current: Denmark has a reputation for English-language higher education, and at master's level that reputation is earned. At bachelor's level it is not. The University of Copenhagen — the country's largest and best known university — teaches all 78 of its bachelor programmes in Danish, and most Danish bachelor's degrees are the same. The English-taught bachelor's offering is real, and it is a specific and fairly narrow set of programmes rather than a choice you can make freely across the country. current:
Quota 1 is national and mechanical: your converted grade average against a published cut-off. Quota 2 is not. The national agency's position is that quota 2 places are allocated "according to criteria published by the institution", which means each institution decides what counts and the criteria genuinely differ between them.

The practical consequence is that there is no general Danish quota 2 strategy to follow, and advice that describes one is describing a single institution. Aalborg states plainly that motivational letters and recommendations are not considered relevant to its quota 2 assessment. Copenhagen Business School requires a motivational essay. Southern Denmark uses an admissions test. Those are three different answers to the same question, all correct, at three universities in one small country.

Check the quota 2 page of the specific programme you want, and treat anything more general than that as background.
note: Danish quota system.

current:
A student arriving from the Danish system will look for the table that turns IB points into a local average, and there is not one. Nuffic describes the IB scale and states that a full Diploma is comparable to a VWO diploma, and stops there.

That is not an omission, it is a different design. Dutch admission to a non-selective programme is an entitlement: hold a qualifying diploma, apply by the deadline, and you are in. Where demand exceeds places, the institution runs its own selection on its own criteria, which may weigh grades alongside a motivation letter, a test or an interview. So the question shifts from "what average do I need" to "is this programme selective, and what does that institution actually select on".

current:
Norway passes every test a Danish IB student would apply to a destination. No tuition, an hour from Copenhagen, a qualification that converts cleanly, a familiar culture and favourable SU treatment. And then most students discover that several of the largest universities teach no bachelor programme in English at all.

The useful way to read that is not as a closed door but as a choice with a known price. For an IB applicant, Samordna opptak counts Danish A at grade 3 or better as documented Norwegian, and a Danish speaker reads Norwegian from the first day. Doing so turns Norway from a handful of English-taught programmes into an entire national system, free of charge. A student who will not is choosing between a very small number of options.

current:
Sweden runs two admissions rounds and they are not two chances at the same thing. The first opens in October and closes on 15 January; it is aimed at applicants from abroad and carries the most English-taught programmes. The second closes on 15 April, and the authority says many English-taught programmes are no longer available in it.

For a May 2027 IB candidate the order is reversed. University Admissions says that if you have not completed your IB Diploma you should not apply to the first round, because it cannot assess you in time without the diploma. Your round is the second, with your IB results due to University Admissions by 5 July through the IB Result Service. So shortlist programmes that are still open in the second round, and treat the January round as closed to you unless a programme, like Stockholm School of Economics, says it admits on predicted grades.

current: China has no UCAS, no Common App and no ministry-run deadline for international undergraduates. The gaokao, which is the national examination the whole Chinese calendar bends around, is not a route a Danish IB candidate takes at all; international applicants are admitted by each university under its own 申请-审核 (application and review) procedure, on its own dates. Two things follow that the rest of this page depends on. First, every date below belongs to one institution and nothing generalises from it. Second, China runs two intakes — a September one, which is the main one and the one this page covers, and a separate February or March spring intake which a smaller number of programmes offer. "2027 entry" on this page means September 2027 unless an entry says otherwise, and a deadline you find on a Chinese university's site may belong to the spring intake and be eight months out of step with the one you want. Check which intake a date is for before you plan around it. Note also that China's joint-venture universities — Duke Kunshan, NYU Shanghai, Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool, Nottingham Ningbo, CUHK-Shenzhen, United International College, Wenzhou-Kean — run on an entirely different calendar from Tsinghua, Peking, Fudan and Shanghai Jiao Tong, and several run on the American one.

current: A lead time, not a date anyone publishes, which is why it carries no day. uni-assist states that you "will usually receive your evaluation result in 4 to 6 weeks", counted from the day it receives your online form, and that applications are evaluated in order of arrival. Its regional table - keyed to where your certificates were issued, not where you live - puts "Western Europe and Latin America: 3-4 weeks", the slowest band on the list, which is the one a Danish IB diploma falls into. The VPD section itself gives no processing figure at all and says only to apply as early as possible. uni-assist's own recommendation is to apply "at least 8 weeks before the deadline expires" so that it can tell you in time if a document is missing. With IB results on 6 July and a 15 July university deadline, that is impossible to do on results - so start the uni-assist file in spring 2027 with predicted grades and school documents.

current: Hungary does have a central admissions system, and it is not the one an IB student from Denmark normally uses: felvi.hu / E-felvételi handles Hungarian-language and state-funded places, while the English-taught programmes on this page are applied for directly to each university. felvi states the rule in Hungarian rather than publishing a 2027 date: "a szeptemberben induló képzésekre vonatkozó általános felvételi eljárás meghirdetései legkésőbb az előző év december 31-ig jelennek meg honlapunkon, a jelentkezési határidő többnyire a rákövetkező év február 15-én jár le" - the programmes are announced by 31 December of the previous year at the latest and the application deadline usually falls on 15 February, with the point thresholds (ponthatárok) set in July. "Többnyire" is felvi’s own hedge, which is why no date is recorded. current: How ISEE works for a foreign family: ISEE is an Italian means-test combining household income (from two years before), savings and property, divided by a scale based on household size. Because your family's income and property are in Denmark, you cannot get an ordinary ISEE. Instead you request an ISEE parificato (also written ISEEU parificato) from an affiliated Italian tax-assistance centre, a CAF. You supply household composition, each member's income for the second preceding year, certificates for any property owned on 31 December, and any securities or shareholdings. Foreign documents must be legalised by an Italian diplomatic or consular representation and accompanied by a certified Italian translation. The CAF sends the result straight to the university. If you skip this step, the university assumes you are wealthy and bills the top bracket.

current: As an EU citizen you use your Danish European Health Insurance Card. The national portal states that a valid passport, student identity card and a valid EHIC entitle the holder to medical care free of charge in Poland. Polish residence law also expressly accepts entitlement under EU coordination rules as satisfying the health insurance condition for a student's right of residence. Two cautions: an EHIC is designed for medically necessary treatment during a temporary stay rather than as long-term cover for a resident student, and Polish universities commonly expect either voluntary National Health Fund (NFZ) insurance or private cover. Non-EU students sign a voluntary NFZ agreement costing about 15 EUR a month. The NFZ premium and enrolment route for an EU student are not confirmed here; ask your university. Source: https://study.gov.pl/health-insurance

current: For the first three months you need do nothing beyond holding a valid travel or identity document, under article 15 of the 2006 act on entry and residence of EU citizens. Beyond three months you have a right of residence as a student under article 16(3) provided you have sufficient funds not to become a burden on social assistance and you have health insurance - and the article expressly accepts entitlement under EU social security coordination, which is the EHIC route, so your Danish blue card satisfies it. Article 20(1) then obliges you to register your residence, which you do at the voivodeship office for where you live. The national portal says EU students should apply for registration within 90 days of arrival and are issued a cost-free certificate of registration. The detailed procedure, forms and processing time are not confirmed here; ask the voivodeship office. Sources: https://study.gov.pl/visa-application and https://lexlege.pb.pl/ustawa-o-wjezdzie-na-terytorium-rzeczypospolitej-polskiej-pobycie-oraz-wyjezdzie-z-tego-terytorium-obywateli-panstw-czlonkowskich-unii-europejskiej-i-czlonkow-ich-rodzin/art-20/

current: Portugal has two completely separate front doors, and a Danish student must use the national one. Non-EU students use the Estatuto do Estudante Internacional, apply straight to a university, and pay somewhere between €3,500 and €16,500 a year. EU citizens — including Danes — are legally excluded from that route and must go through the Concurso Nacional de Acesso, the same national contest Portuguese school-leavers use. The payoff is the price: the capped public tuition (propina) was €697 for 2025/26. The catch is that the national contest is built around Portuguese school exams and mostly leads to Portuguese-taught degrees.

current: What you need to know about Early Decision is not when it closes but what signing it costs you. Early Decision I (1 to 15 November 2026) and Early Decision II (early January 2027) are binding in the strongest sense the American system has. Amherst's wording is that you agree not to be an Early Decision candidate anywhere else and, if admitted, to withdraw your applications from every other college and enrol. It is a signed agreement — student, parent and school counsellor — filed inside the Common App for one college only. Two consequences follow and neither is obvious from a calendar. First, an admitted Early Decision applicant does not get the 1 May reply date: that decision was made in November. Second, and for a Danish family paying from abroad this is usually the more expensive loss, you can never compare financial aid offers, because you will only ever hold one. Early Action, Restrictive Early Action and Single-Choice Early Action are NOT binding — you keep every offer and still reply on 1 May — but Stanford's and Yale's restrict where else you may apply early, so they still decide your whole autumn in October. Missing an early round costs you that round's higher admit rate; signing an Early Decision agreement costs you the choice.

current: Each institution's aid deadline is its own, and at most of them it is the application deadline itself. Grinnell states that "All financial aid forms must be submitted by the same deadline as the Common Application". Macalester states that "financial aid cannot be awarded after an offer of admission has been made, nor at any time during their studies at Macalester" — that is a door that closes permanently, not a late penalty. Bowdoin's Regular Decision aid deadline is 1 February, a month after its application date. MIT's two aid dates, 30 November and 15 February, have entries of their own. A family that applies first and asks about money in the spring has forfeited the money. Which form: as a Danish citizen you file the CSS Profile, not the FAFSA. The FAFSA is the United States federal aid application and federal aid requires US citizenship or eligible-non-citizen status, which an F-1 student visa is not — so every FAFSA date you will meet on American admissions pages, including the 1 October opening and the 2 March deadline printed on the University of California's own dates page, is not yours. Grinnell asks for "the 2027-28 CSS Profile"; Macalester asks for the CSS Profile "OR the 2027-2028 International Student Application for Financial Assistance (ISAFA)" and points international applicants who cannot afford the CSS Profile fee at the free ISAFA instead, because neither college waives the CSS Profile fee for international applicants. The CSS Profile itself carries no national deadline — the colleges set them, typically 1 or 15 November for the early rounds and January to February for Regular Decision. The College Board had not published the 2027-28 opening date on 23 September 2026; the customary opening is 1 October of the preceding year. Open the CSS Profile in early October 2026 and check the date yourself.

current: Korea's Ministry of Education divides higher education into more kinds than English-language guides usually show. Alongside the four-year 대학교 that every foreigner has heard of sit 전문대학 junior colleges, national 교육대학 for primary teachers, the special-law science and technology institutes, polytechnic colleges under the labour ministry rather than this one, and open and cyber universities. An IB Diploma opens the first three of those; the junior college is rarely mentioned to foreigners and is the nearest Korean relative of the Danish erhvervsakademi.

current: Korea keeps a separate admissions track for applicants who did all twelve years of school abroad, and an IB Diploma fits it: no Suneung, a small international pool, and a decision on transcript, essays and often an interview. The catch is the calendar. The Korean year begins in March, and March 2027 is out of reach for a May 2027 candidate, so the real choices are September 2027 on predicted grades or March 2028 with results. English-taught degrees are concentrated at Yonsei's Underwood International College, KAIST, POSTECH, UNIST and GIST, plus specific divisions elsewhere.
note: No audience assumption.

current: MODEL FRICTION, all of it in src/ and none of it worked around in the data. (1) src/lib/canonical.mjs denormalise() understands only kind 'local-equivalency', so a requirement written in IB terms projects to entryRequirements: null and a Dutch programme page renders the heading 'And one of these combinations' above an empty list. ADR 0002 added the ib-subject path to the schema and to the engine; this projection into the page templates was not updated with it. (2) The same projection builds extraRequirements from the requirement kinds essay/test/portfolio/interview/audition/other without consulting `mandatory`, so a Selection Factor renders on the programme page under 'On top of the subjects' as though it were an entry requirement. On the Erasmus IBA page a student sees 'Your grade average — 75 per cent of the selection score' in the same list as things they must hold. The answer to 'can a student tell a Requirement from a Selection Factor on the page' is currently no. (3) assess() returns selection.factors and nothing renders it; admission.capacityNote is not rendered anywhere, so numerus fixus capacity and the hard 15 January date reach a page only through an Application Route milestone. (4) The restricted-admission note on a programme page is Danish copy — it talks about quota cut-offs and national intake policy — and it now appears on Dutch pages. (5) src/pages/programmes.mjs describes the planner as checking 'every English-taught programme in Denmark' and converting subjects 'using the Danish Agency's official table'; it now also checks sixteen Dutch ones and converts nothing for them.

All four English-taught bachelor's degrees have restricted admission. Quota 1 ranks applicants with convertible qualifications purely on the converted grade point average. Applicants whose grades cannot be converted to the Danish scale are assessed only in quota 2. AAU publishes the previous year's quota figure on each programme page, and 'All Admitted' means everyone qualified was offered a place that year.

Roskilde University was set up in 1972 to experiment with how knowledge is taught, and it still works differently from every other Danish university. You do not apply to a named subject. You apply to one of three broad international bachelor programmes, spend the whole first year in an interdisciplinary basic studies section, and only then choose the two bachelor subjects you will study for the remaining two years. Roughly half of all study time is group project work on real problems rather than lectures and exams, and the campus at Trekroner, 30 minutes by train from Copenhagen, has about 7,900 students.

Sønderborg holds eleven of SDU's fifteen fully English-taught bachelor's degrees. It is a small town on the island of Als in the far south of Jutland, closer to Flensburg in Germany than to any large Danish city, and several hours from Copenhagen by train. The campus, Alsion, is a single modern building shared with a concert hall, and the student body there is strongly international — partly because Danish applicants mostly do not move that far south. Mads Clausen's company Danfoss is based next door, which is why so much of the engineering sits here.

Vejle is SDU's newest campus and holds four English-taught degrees, all of them IT. SDU calls it "Denmark's newest IT campus". Vejle is a mid-sized town on the east coast of Jutland on the main motorway and rail line, with a cluster of IT employers nearby, so student jobs are realistic.

current: The single most important fact about the University of Copenhagen, for anyone finishing an IB, is that you cannot study there at bachelor level without fluent academic Danish. UCPH says it plainly on its own bachelor page: "UCPH only offers bachelor's degree programmes taught in Danish." All 78 bachelor's degrees are in Danish; the English-taught offering begins at master's level. It is Denmark's oldest and largest university, founded in 1479, with about 36,800 students across six faculties and four campuses in and around central Copenhagen — and if you want it, you need to plan a Danish-language route into it years in advance, not in your final IB year.
Applying in quota 2 commits you to the quota 2 test and an interview held in Danish, Norwegian or Swedish.

There is a hard grade floor: "In addition to having accomplished an IB Diploma, you must present a grade point average equivalent to the Danish 6.0 – or more." Below a converted 6.0 you cannot be considered in quota 1.

Danish language is a requirement for every bachelor's degree. If your A HL/SL or B HL Language or Literature subject is not Danish, Norwegian or Swedish, you must pass Studieprøven i dansk som andetsprog or document equivalent academic Danish. Danish B at HL normally exempts you.

Studieprøven has four parts — oral, listening, reading and written — and "must be passed with at least grade 02 in each of all the 3 examination disciplines". Medicine, Dentistry and Dental Hygiene require grade 7 rather than 02 in each discipline. Alternatively you can pass a supplementary upper secondary course in Danish A.
Students from the Nordic countries with Danish, Norwegian or Swedish in their upper secondary education do not have to sit a Danish language test.

Subject conversion follows the Danish Agency's handbook: IB Mathematics HL/SL counts as Matematik A/B, Physics HL/SL as Fysik A/B, English A1/A2 at SL or HL as Engelsk A, and Danish A1 HL as the Danish requirement.

A, B and C are Danish subject levels, not grades. The 6.0 is a grade point average on the Danish 7-point scale.

current: DP Course Results (formerly the IB Certificate) of at least 18 points, with at least grade 3 in all six subjects and at least three subjects at HL, are a qualifying examination in Denmark on the same terms as a two-year hf without overbygning: they give access to erhvervsakademi- and professionsbachelor programmes through quota 1 and quota 2, and to a university bachelor only after two successive raises of upper-secondary subject level, at least one to A level, taken as hf-enkeltfag. Course Results under 18 points, or containing any subject at grade 1 or 2, are not a qualifying examination at all. A full IB Diploma of 24 points or more gives access to every higher education programme in Denmark.
note: Danish qualification rule.

current: This is the rule that decides whether a Course candidate can apply at all, and it is national: the Agency sets which examinations are adgangsgivende and every Danish institution applies the same one, so it is recorded once here and referenced from each Opportunity rather than restated per institution. No institution page read for this catalogue states it. The Agency says in as many words that IB Certificate is the former designation for DP Course Results, which is why this site uses Course Results throughout: "Samme vilkår gælder for ansøgere med IB Certificate, som er den tidligere betegnelse for Diploma Programme (DP) Course Results." current: The friendliest Japanese calendar we found for an IB candidate, and the reason is Period III. It closes on 7 April 2027, by which point a May 2027 candidate's predicted grades are settled and their mock results exist, and it announces on 24 May — still before the diploma, but after the exams. Keio also says in as many words that predicted grades are acceptable, which most Japanese programmes leave to inference. The trade is that the three periods share one quota of about 100 places, so a later period is competing for what the earlier ones did not take. Applying in Period I is the stronger position; applying in Period III is the one that fits the Danish school year.

current: Read for what it does and does not reach. The mandatory limb of lid 2 is about a DIPLOMA and cannot reach a Course Result. The Lisbon limb of lid 1 is different in kind: it turns on whether the applicant HAS ACCESS to higher education in a convention country rather than on what document they hold, and Denmark — where this site's readers sit their IB — publishes in as many words that DP Course Results of at least 18 points with grade 3 in all six subjects give access to Danish erhvervsakademi and professionsbachelor programmes. A Danish-resident Course candidate therefore has an argument under this limb that a candidate with no such access does not have. It is an argument and not an entitlement: the same sentence preserves the institution's power under article IV.1 of the convention to show a substantial difference between the access rules in the awarding country and the Dutch ones, and 'access to hbo in Denmark' against 'access to wo in the Netherlands' is exactly the kind of difference an institution may point at. No Dutch institution page read for this catalogue mentions the limb at all. It is recorded because a route that exists in the statute and is never advertised is precisely what a Course candidate cannot find alone, and it must be raised with the admissions office in writing, early, and in those terms.
note: Correct location framing ('where this site's readers sit their IB', 'Danish-resident').

current: This is the door the Netherlands actually publishes for someone without a qualifying diploma, and three things about it decide whether it is any use to an IB Course candidate. First, the age: twenty-one. A student who leaves school at eighteen with Course Results does not qualify for two or three years, and lid 3 makes the exceptions discretionary — the institution MAY waive the age limit, and the first of its two grounds is a foreign DIPLOMA that gives access at home, which a Course Result is not, leaving only the 'bijzondere gevallen' clause. Second, the language: the statute requires the committee to find sufficient command of DUTCH, which is a strange fit with the English-taught bachelor programmes this catalogue lists, and no institution page read for this catalogue explains how the two meet. Third, it is per programme and per institution: lid 2 puts the requirements in each programme's own onderwijs- en examenregeling, so there is no national syllabus and no national result, and passing one does not carry to another programme. None of this makes it a route a Course candidate can plan on at eighteen, and that is the finding rather than a gap in it.

current: Two of these dates are the single most consequential thing on this page for a Danish candidate sitting the May 2027 session, and both fall before results exist. The mid-year route - which is the only way to start in 2027 rather than waiting until February 2028 - closes to international applicants on 8 June 2027, and closes a month later for domestic ones, so the earlier date is specifically ours. And the competitive health programmes for the following February close on 1 July 2027, days before IB results are published. Neither is a date a student would find by looking for a national deadline, because there is not one; both are a single university's dates, published on that university's own page, and the other seven universities will have their own. The lesson generalises even where the numbers do not: in New Zealand the deadline that matters is the one on the programme page, and for an international applicant it is frequently earlier than the domestic one.

DTU is Denmark's main technical university, on a large purpose-built campus in Kongens Lyngby about 15 km north of central Copenhagen. Almost all of its teaching is engineering and natural science, and its undergraduate degrees are mostly taught in Danish. For an IB student the practical point is that DTU has exactly one full English-taught bachelor's degree, General Engineering, where roughly 60 per cent of the students come from outside Denmark.

Roskilde University was set up in 1972 to experiment with how knowledge is taught, and it still works differently from every other Danish university. You do not apply to a named subject. You apply to one of three broad international bachelor programmes, spend the whole first year in an interdisciplinary basic studies section, and only then choose the two bachelor subjects you will study for the remaining two years. Roughly half of all study time is group project work on real problems rather than lectures and exams, and the campus at Trekroner, 30 minutes by train from Copenhagen, has about 7,900 students.
Danish

SDU is spread across seven towns in the south and west of Denmark, and where you study matters more here than at any other Danish university. Its headquarters and most of its Danish-taught teaching are in Odense, but almost every fully English-taught bachelor's degree sits in Sønderborg, a small town on the island of Als by the German border, or in Vejle, SDU's newest campus and an IT-focused one. SDU is also unusual in how it admits people: an aptitude test called uniTEST is used for quota 2 on nearly all programmes, and SDU openly recommends that everyone sit it, including applicants whose grades would be good enough for quota 1.
Danish

Sønderborg holds eleven of SDU's fifteen fully English-taught bachelor's degrees. It is a small town on the island of Als in the far south of Jutland, closer to Flensburg in Germany than to any large Danish city, and several hours from Copenhagen by train. The campus, Alsion, is a single modern building shared with a concert hall, and the student body there is strongly international — partly because Danish applicants mostly do not move that far south. Mads Clausen's company Danfoss is based next door, which is why so much of the engineering sits here.

Vejle is SDU's newest campus and holds four English-taught degrees, all of them IT. SDU calls it "Denmark's newest IT campus". Vejle is a mid-sized town on the east coast of Jutland on the main motorway and rail line, with a cluster of IT employers nearby, so student jobs are realistic.

Odense is SDU's headquarters and Denmark's third-largest city, half an hour from Copenhagen by fast train — but only one fully English-taught bachelor's degree is taught there, Market and Management Anthropology. If you want Odense and you do not speak Danish, your options are almost nil at bachelor level.

SDU also has campuses in Kolding, Esbjerg, Slagelse and Copenhagen. None of them currently offers a fully English-taught bachelor's degree, so they are not options for an IB student who does not read Danish.

Robot Systems (Robotteknologi) in Odense is often assumed to be English-taught. It is not: SDU lists its tuition language as Danish. Robotics in English at SDU means Mechatronics in Sønderborg at bachelor level.

International Business Administration, Language and Culture (Sønderborg and EUF Flensborg) is listed among SDU's international programmes but is excluded here: SDU gives its tuition language as "English, German and Danish" and it requires Danish level A plus German at A or B level. It took only 6 students in 2026.
A, B and C are Danish subject levels, not grades. SDU repeats this on every programme page: "A is advanced, B is intermediate, and C is beginner level."

It does not close this one to you. The Danish Agency treats DP Course Results of at least 18 points, with at least grade 3 in all six subjects and at least three of them at HL, as equivalent to a qualifying examination for a Danish university bachelor once you have added two successive raises in the level of upper-secondary subjects, at least one of them to A level, taken as hf-enkeltfag or as a self-study candidate. If you already hold an A-level subject other than Danish, two raises to B level are enough. Retaking to be awarded the full IB Diploma is the other published route.

The rule is national rather than this university's: the Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science sets which examinations are adgangsgivende, and every Danish institution applies the same one. Two things about it are easy to get wrong. GSK (gymnasial supplering) cannot be used for this — GSK raises a subject level for someone who already holds a qualifying examination, so it meets a specific subject requirement but never raises the level of the examination itself. And the average used in quota 1 is the one from the first qualifying examination, so a Course Results holder who supplements or retakes is still converted on the original Course Results result.

current: Non-EU tuition at institution level: Academic year 2026/2027, per year (60 ECTS): EUR 13,000 for Cognitive Science and for Economics and Business Administration in both Aarhus and Herning; EUR 17,300 for Computer Science, Data Science and IT Product Development. Application fee EUR 150 (DKK 1,125) per applicant, payable by 15 March and refunded only if you enrol and are still enrolled on 1 October. AU states: "Aarhus University does not offer scholarships for any of our Bachelor's degree programmes." EU/EEA and Swiss citizens pay nothing.

Specific admission requirements: You must fulfil the following specific admission requirements: English B. Mathematics B. History B or History of Ideas B or Social Studies B or Contemporary History B. B-level is the Danish subject level, not the grade. Grade point Average (GPA) requirement of 6.0 in quota 1: You must have a minimum GPA of 6.0 on the Danish 7-point grading scale in your qualifying examination to be assessed in quota 1.

It does not close this one to you. The Danish Agency treats DP Course Results of at least 18 points, with at least grade 3 in all six subjects and at least three of them at HL, as equivalent to a qualifying examination for a Danish university bachelor once you have added two successive raises in the level of upper-secondary subjects, at least one of them to A level, taken as hf-enkeltfag or as a self-study candidate. If you already hold an A-level subject other than Danish, two raises to B level are enough. Retaking to be awarded the full IB Diploma is the other published route.

The rule is national rather than this university's: the Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science sets which examinations are adgangsgivende, and every Danish institution applies the same one. Two things about it are easy to get wrong. GSK (gymnasial supplering) cannot be used for this — GSK raises a subject level for someone who already holds a qualifying examination, so it meets a specific subject requirement but never raises the level of the examination itself. And the average used in quota 1 is the one from the first qualifying examination, so a Course Results holder who supplements or retakes is still converted on the original Course Results result.

current: Which IB award opens this one IS established, and it is the opposite answer from SDU's university bachelor programmes. SDU's own IB page splits its rule by programme type and accepts DP Course Results (or an IB Certificate) for a Bachelor of Engineering with all six subjects at grade 3 and three at HL, with no supplementary hf-enkeltfag — where the same page requires two supplementary subjects for a bachelor's programme. Read 2026-09-23 at https://www.sdu.dk/en/uddannelse/bachelor/bachelor-admission/admission-requirements/educational-background/international-baccalaureate . The national rule behind it was confirmed the same day from SDU's Danish list of qualifying examinations, https://www.sdu.dk/da/uddannelse/ansoegning-optagelse/bachelor-diplomingenioer/adgangskrav/adgangsgivende-eksamener , which names hf uden overbygning as qualifying only for diplomingeniør programmes, and from DTU's equivalent page, which states the same restriction. This replaces the earlier note on this record, which left the question unrecorded because the Agency's guidance names programme types rather than this hybrid. Both SDU pages return their content to a plain fetch; the Danish page has no /international-baccalaureate child (404), so the English page is the only SDU page that states the IB rule.

In addition you must have passed: English level B. Mathematics level A. Physics level B or Geoscience level A. Course levels refer to the Danish high school system: A is advanced, B is intermediate, and C is beginner level.

SDU publishes two different IB rules on one page, and the difference between them is the whole point. For a bachelor's programme it asks a Course candidate to have "supplemented with at least two individual subjects (minimum one at A-level subject and one at B-level subject)". For a Bachelor of Engineering it asks for nothing beyond the six subjects at grade 3 with three at HL. So a Course candidate reaches this programme with the award as it stands, and no hf-enkeltfag are needed. The national order underneath that: the Danish Agency treats DP Course Results of at least 18 points as equal to a two-year hf without overbygning, and an hf without overbygning is adgangsgivende to a diplomingeniør-uddannelse but not to a universitetsbacheloruddannelse. SDU's own Danish list of qualifying examinations says exactly that — "Eksamener, der kun giver adgang til diplomingeniøruddannelser: Højere forberedelseseksamen (hf) uden overbygning aflagt efter gymnasiereformen 2017" — and DTU publishes the same restriction for its own diplomingeniør intake. Two things this does not do. It does not waive the subject requirements below: Mathematics A, English B and Physics B or Geoscience A still bind, and a Course candidate meets them with IB subjects on the same conversion as anybody else. And the 18-point floor recorded here is the Agency's rather than SDU's: below 18 points, or with any subject at grade 1 or 2, the Course Results are not a qualifying examination at all and no Danish programme is reachable. Grade 3 in all six subjects already puts the subject total at 18, so the two conditions meet in the same place.
Quota 1 GPA floor of 7.0 on the Danish scale.

SDU's own IB page splits its rule by programme type and accepts DP Course Results (or an IB Certificate) for a Bachelor of Engineering with all six subjects at grade 3 and three at HL, with no supplementary hf-enkeltfag — where the same page requires two supplementary subjects for a bachelor's programme. Read 2026-09-23 at https://www.sdu.dk/en/uddannelse/bachelor/bachelor-admission/admission-requirements/educational-background/international-baccalaureate . The national rule behind it was confirmed the same day from SDU's Danish list of qualifying examinations, https://www.sdu.dk/da/uddannelse/ansoegning-optagelse/bachelor-diplomingenioer/adgangskrav/adgangsgivende-eksamener , which names hf uden overbygning as qualifying only for diplomingeniør programmes, and from DTU's equivalent page, which states the same restriction. This replaces the earlier note on this record, which left the question unrecorded because the Agency's guidance names programme types rather than this hybrid. Both SDU pages return their content to a plain fetch; the Danish page has no /international-baccalaureate child (404), so the English page is the only SDU page that states the IB rule.

SDU publishes two different IB rules on one page, and the difference between them is the whole point. For a bachelor's programme it asks a Course candidate to have "supplemented with at least two individual subjects (minimum one at A-level subject and one at B-level subject)". For a Bachelor of Engineering it asks for nothing beyond the six subjects at grade 3 with three at HL. So a Course candidate reaches this programme with the award as it stands, and no hf-enkeltfag are needed. The national order underneath that: the Danish Agency treats DP Course Results of at least 18 points as equal to a two-year hf without overbygning, and an hf without overbygning is adgangsgivende to a diplomingeniør-uddannelse but not to a universitetsbacheloruddannelse. SDU's own Danish list of qualifying examinations says exactly that — "Eksamener, der kun giver adgang til diplomingeniøruddannelser: Højere forberedelseseksamen (hf) uden overbygning aflagt efter gymnasiereformen 2017" — and DTU publishes the same restriction for its own diplomingeniør intake. Two things this does not do. It does not waive the subject requirements below: Mathematics A, English B and Physics B or Geoscience A still bind, and a Course candidate meets them with IB subjects on the same conversion as anybody else. And the 18-point floor recorded here is the Agency's rather than SDU's: below 18 points, or with any subject at grade 1 or 2, the Course Results are not a qualifying examination at all and no Danish programme is reachable. Grade 3 in all six subjects already puts the subject total at 18, so the two conditions meet in the same place.
Quota 1 GPA floor of 7.0 on the Danish scale.

Denmark lets you top up a missing level through gymnasial supplering, taken at a VUC or GSK centre. Two things to know before you plan around it: the courses are taught in Danish, and GSK can only meet a specific subject requirement — it cannot raise your overall qualification level.

If you hold a full IB Diploma your qualification level is already fine, so GSK is exactly the right tool for a missing Mathematics A. If you hold DP Course Results rather than a Diploma, GSK is the wrong tool entirely. Your qualification level is not yet university-bachelor standard, and the Agency says plainly that GSK cannot raise it — that takes hf-enkeltfag, or sitting the subjects as a self-study candidate. Taking a GSK course in that situation costs you a term and changes nothing. GSK is still the right tool for a specific subject requirement at an erhvervsakademi or professionsbachelor programme, and a subject taken for that stays valid if you later switch to a university bachelor.

Free tuition and an expensive city can easily cost more than modest tuition somewhere cheap. Norway charges no tuition and budgets NOK 15,488 a month to live. Copenhagen is the most expensive place to be a student in Denmark by a distance, and several strong English-taught programmes are in cities that cost half as much.

If you are a Danish citizen, work out early whether SU follows you. It does, for a full degree abroad. In another Nordic country you get SU and loans exactly as if you studied in Denmark — which, for anyone starting from 2025, means the prescribed length of the programme and no more. Elsewhere, at most four years (48 klip).

Everything on this site is a description. Sønderborg and Copenhagen are both in Denmark and are not remotely the same experience, and no amount of careful prose substitutes for standing in a place for an afternoon.

Open days are the obvious route. Failing that, a train ticket and a wander is cheap compared to three years somewhere you did not want to be.
Decide whether you need Danish at A level

Most Danish bachelor's degrees are taught in Danish and require Danish at A level. If you took Danish A1 or Danish A Literature at either level you already have it. If you did not, and you want a Danish-taught programme, you will need Studieprøven i dansk or an equivalent.

This is the single biggest constraint on studying in Denmark with an IB, and it is rarely stated as a headline. The University of Copenhagen teaches every one of its bachelor's degrees in Danish.

Danish applications close on 15 March and IB results are not released until 6 July. The mechanism that resolves this is the IB's own results service: your coordinator registers you and your results travel directly to up to six institutions.

Get a receipt. This is administrative rather than academic, and it is the single most common way an otherwise complete application fails.

Tests are required rather than optional wherever they appear, and their registration deadlines sit well before the application deadlines — UAT-UK for Oxford and Cambridge closes in late September, two and a half weeks before the UCAS deadline in mid-October. Austria's MedAT registration closes in March for a July test, roughly a year before results.

SDU in Denmark uses the uniTEST for quota 2. Italy uses TOLC and IMAT. Central European medical schools run their own entrance exams, several of which can be sat online from Denmark.

Copenhagen Business School requires one on all six of its English-taught programmes. The Dutch numerus fixus selection procedures usually include something similar. US applications are built around it.

One sharp caveat for a May 2027 IB candidate applying to CBS: its essay only counts in the Danish quota 2 round if at least three months have passed since you finished school. If you apply straight from the IB, your essay does not count. That is the kind of rule that makes the difference between a considered application and a wasted one.

Many Danish institutions count documented relevant work or education in quota 2 — Aalborg, for example, counts up to twelve months. The documentation has to be specific: an employer's statement giving your responsibilities, the period of employment, weekly hours and a signature.

Aalborg is refreshingly blunt that motivational letters and recommendations are *not* considered relevant in its quota 2 and are not required. Other institutions differ. Check the one you want rather than assuming.

In systems with holistic admissions — the US most of all, and UK personal statements to a lesser degree — sustained depth in one or two things reads far better than a long list. Admissions officers read thousands of these and can tell the difference between a commitment and a collection.

In most of Europe this has no effect whatsoever. Danish quota 1 is grades alone, and quota 2 counts documented work rather than interests. Do not build an activity portfolio for a European application; it will not be read.

CAS is required by the IB and by essentially no university. No admissions office in Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Germany or the Netherlands will read it. Treating it as an admissions instrument is a misunderstanding that costs students a lot of stress for nothing.

What it is genuinely good for: finding out whether you like something before you commit three years to it. A student who volunteers in a hospital and discovers they cannot stand it has learned something far more valuable than a line on a form. That is worth doing deliberately.

The standard Danish business economics degree — financing, economics, marketing, strategy and organisation — taught in English in Aalborg, with each semester built around a project done with or about a real company. It is the only one of AAU's English-taught bachelor's degrees that is not an engineering degree, and the only one based in Aalborg.

Engineering for biotechnological production: using cells and microorganisms to make medicines, food and fuels, and to treat waste water. It is taught in Kalundborg with Novo Nordisk, Novonesis and Lundbeck nearby, and includes a five-month internship. Needs Maths A, Physics B, Chemistry B and English B, and every quota 2 applicant is interviewed.

Mathematics, statistics and programming aimed squarely at getting reliable answers out of very large datasets. It sits between computer science and statistics and is the right choice if the appeal is the analysis rather than the systems engineering. AU states that the English-taught version is intended for international students and that it is academically equivalent to the Danish-taught Datavidenskab.

The standard Danish business economics degree taught in English: how a company's activities can be analysed and managed so they create value, and how to build strategies for growth. All teaching and all reading is in English because the programme is built around international business. It is the broadest of AU's English-taught degrees and the usual route into AU's business master's programmes.

The broad business economics degree — strategy, finance, marketing, organisation — with everything framed around companies operating across borders. About half the compulsory courses use mathematics as a working tool, at roughly the level of the entry requirement. It is the most applied-to and the highest cut-off of any CBS bachelor, and a third of the students are non-Danish.

A small, highly structured degree about the industry that moves physical goods: shipping markets, chartering, maritime law, logistics and trade finance. The second year includes a compulsory semester abroad in Singapore, Hong Kong or Greece, and the final year includes a compulsory internship in a shipping company. Only 75 places, and half of them are decided in quota 2.

A broad engineering degree that starts with heavy maths, physics and chemistry and then narrows into one of four specialisations: Living Systems, Advanced Materials, Cyber Systems or Future Energy. About 60 per cent of the students are international, so it suits you if you want an engineering degree in English without having to pick your exact branch at 17.

A medical degree is not the same thing as a licence to work as a doctor. In Denmark the licence is called autorisation, and the right to work without supervision is called tilladelse til selvstaendigt virke. Both are granted by Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed.

The good news is that EU law is on your side. Under Directive 2005/36/EC on the recognition of professional qualifications, a medical qualification listed in Annex V point 5.1.1 is recognised automatically across the EU. Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed states plainly that you can get Danish authorisation and permission to practise independently if you are a citizen of an EU/EEA country or Switzerland and hold a medical degree from an EU/EEA country or Switzerland. Denmark does not make you repeat the Danish klinisk basisuddannelse in that case, and it does not make you sit a Danish medical exam.

The authority also says that automatic recognition depends on the education, not on the passport: someone who is not an EU citizen but who trained as a doctor in the EU/EEA may still be recognised under the automatic-recognition principles.

current:
This is the single most important thing on this page and it is the thing recruitment agencies do not tell you.

Annex V of the Directive lists, for each country, the qualification that gets automatic recognition and any certificates that must accompany it. For Czechia, Hungary and Estonia, the medical diploma stands alone: no accompanying certificate is listed. For Poland it does not. The Polish entry requires the diploma plus the certificate of the state final medical examination, the Lekarski Egzamin Koncowy (LEK), and Poland's own medical chamber says the certificate of completed postgraduate internship, staz podyplomowy, is also part of what accompanies the Polish diploma.

The Naczelna Izba Lekarska, the Polish chamber of physicians, puts it bluntly: it can only certify full Polish qualifications for EU recognition if you have both the LEK and a recognised postgraduate internship. If you have neither, what you can get instead is an Article 23 or 27 certificate of conformity, and the chamber says that certificate does not confirm that a graduate of a Polish university has obtained full qualifications to practise the profession in Poland.

In plain terms: if you graduate in Poland, come straight home and skip the LEK and the internship, you are not in the automatic-recognition track. You can still work towards Danish authorisation, but you are on a slower and less certain path.

current:
Denmark has a fallback for exactly this situation. The regional postgraduate training secretariats run what they call a KBU-lignende forlob, a KBU-like programme, for doctors trained inside the EU, EEA and the Nordic countries who have not been granted automatic authorisation. Doctors trained outside the EU/EEA go through a longer route of evalueringsansaettelser, evaluation posts of at least two times six months.

So the fallback exists, but it costs you time and it depends on getting a post. It is much better to graduate with the full set of documents than to arrive home and negotiate.

There is no formal Danish language test imposed by Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed on doctors trained inside the EU. Under EU law the authority has to issue the authorisation on the basis of the qualification. Danish language competence is treated as the employer's responsibility, and Danish hospitals do check it.

That cuts both ways. Legally you are fine. Practically, a Danish hospital will not hire you if your clinical Danish is weak, and if you have spent six years working in Polish, Hungarian or Czech, your Danish medical vocabulary will be thin. Danish doctors' organisations have publicly argued for a formal language test for EU-trained doctors; that has not become law, but it tells you what employers think.

Keep your Danish alive while you are away. Do Danish-language clinical placements or summer jobs in Denmark if you can.
